personal.bio: Dual student of Business Informatics (B.Sc.) at FHDW Bielefeld with Deutsche Telekom AG as practice partner, specialising in Software Engineering. Day to day I design and build applications on the Pega Platform — currently rebuilding Telekom's idea-management system, before that migrating HR processes off a legacy system as a business analyst. Off the clock I run my own home server, live in Linux and open source, and use AI tools as part of my everyday development workflow.

caseStudy.name: HomeLabSetup
caseStudy.tagline: A data centre that fits on a shelf.
caseStudy.intro: Twenty-plus self-hosted services on a single Raspberry Pi 5 — media automation, private cloud, photo backup, smart home and full monitoring — reachable from anywhere without a single open port on the router.

blocks.label: Problem
blocks.text: Self-hosting usually ends in one of two places: everything stays locked inside the LAN and is useless on the go, or ports get forwarded and the router becomes an attack surface. On top of that, most home-lab guides stop at the compose file and skip the part where the services actually have to work together.

blocks.label: Approach
blocks.text: Every service runs as Docker Compose on the Pi, behind two access tiers: public apps go out through a Cloudflare Tunnel, admin UIs are reachable only via LAN or a Tailscale mesh — the router has no port forwarding at all. Nginx Proxy Manager terminates SSL, Pi-hole handles DNS, and Authentik puts SSO and 2FA in front of everything. Torrent traffic shares Gluetun's network namespace, so a dropped VPN means no internet for qBittorrent. Storage is split deliberately: databases on the SSD, bulk media on the HDD.

blocks.label: Outcome
blocks.text: Prometheus scrapes every container and the host itself; alerts land in Telegram within minutes, and Watchtower keeps images current. The repo is written as the guide I was missing — architecture diagram, per-service web-UI setup and the security reasoning behind each decision.
